$comment: What each decision record's costs say a user, integrator or operator of a release will meet, one sentence each, or why the record has none. Held to the records by scripts/release-report/limitations.test.mjs: 'reviewed' is the sha256 of the record as it was read, so any edit to a record -- a status line naming a later record included -- fails until it is read again and stamped with 'node scripts/release-report/limitations.mjs --stamp NNNN'. A line can outlive its truth until its record changes; 'heldBy' names a test that shows it still holds, and the release report fails a run in which that test did not pass. The wording is held by review.

limitations.says: Running Formancy Report in production needs a paid licence, and redistributing it inside another product a separate agreement; reading, evaluating, developing and testing it are free.
The `@formancy` scope mixes formancy's Apache-2.0 packages with this module's source-available ones, so a dependency audit reads each package's licence rather than its scope.
No lawyer has reviewed the licence; until one has, it is a statement of intent made carefully, and a customer's production agreement is the document that governs.
The published packages depend on upstream `@formancy/*` at exact versions, so an upstream fix reaches an installation only through a release of this module that moves the version.
Report reads Formancy Data only at the release its provider was built against, 0.1.0, so a Data upgrade reaches a host only through a release of this module that moves the version.

A claim about a rendered PDF rests on its text and images as PDF.js reads them back, an SVG image's painted paths and clip and the pixels around it, and its QR codes as ZXing decodes the page PDF.js draws, so a rule or border through a row, a shape over a line, a clipped glyph or white text on white is not seen until page images are compared.
A text run's box is computed from its baseline and font size, not traced from its glyphs, so an accent that reaches past its box into the line below is not seen.
The report format is version "0", a draft: nothing written under it is promised to be read by a later release, and a report written now may need re-authoring or migrating when the format freezes.
A report of any other `reportSpecVersion` is refused whole, naming both versions, so a document from a newer release fails loudly in an older reader.
The workspace's Node floor of 22.13 is advisory, and what fails on an older Node has not been measured.
pdfmake's fonts and access policies are global to a process, so a host that uses pdfmake for something of its own finds the renderer's configuration in place after every report.
pdfmake keeps rows whole per table, not per row, so one row that cannot be kept whole lets every multi-line row in its table split across pages.

A spacer that does not fit what is left of a page becomes a page break and loses its space, a page-region line that wraps only for some page numbers is not refused, and a run of keep-with-next headings before a page break or the end of the document is not kept together.
A JPEG is checked to its structure only; its scan data is never decoded before it is embedded.

A dependency's licence is read from its declared identifier and a font's from its name table, so code a package vendors under a licence of its own, a font inside a script, and terms that are not what their identifier says are not seen.

The dependency guard reads the tree this repository installed, not what a customer's install resolves: a range resolved afresh, or another platform's optional package, is judged only where CI installs it.
The dependency inventory review owed before the first paid release is still owed; until it is done, the guard's allow-list is the only check.
Version 0 has no positioned elements: a letterhead with a logo at exact coordinates in the page header cannot be drawn, and columns only approximate it.
A report has one detail table over one dataset, with one grouping level, and draws images from its header only, so two lists, subtotals within subtotals, or a photo per row cannot be expressed.
Names an expression reads follow formancy's field keys and every other id is lower case with hyphens, so an author meets two id syntaxes.
A null value prints as nothing; a placeholder such as n/a has to be written as an expression.
Print styles are a small vocabulary of tokens, so a host's theme does not carry over into a report.
A report with one unknown property or a length finer than a hundredth of a point is refused whole, so an editor has to keep the document valid at every step.
The bounds on a report's size are chosen, not measured, so lowering one later would refuse reports that are valid now.
A report's hash rests on `@formancy/spec`'s canonicalisation, so a change there changes every stored hash.
Every commit validates and compares the whole report, so a keystroke in a property field pays a cost that grows with the report, and that cost is not measured.
The session keeps 200 undo steps unless told otherwise, each a whole snapshot, and drops the oldest past them; 200 is chosen, not measured.
Renaming a style that components use takes a transaction -- a new style, the components changed and the old style removed -- because no single command passes through an invalid report.
In a patch, `null` removes a value and `undefined` changes nothing.
A listener that throws makes the edit's caller see the exception after the edit has happened, and the outcome it would have returned is lost.
Snapshots do not merge, so two people editing one draft conflict, and the second save is refused by its hash.
An expression is checked against the types of what it reads, so `dec(row.amount)` is a type error when the amount already is a decimal.
A decimal that may be null cannot be compared with `==`; equality is written as two orderings.
`has()` on a member is refused: every member is bound, null when empty, so `!= null` asks instead.
`now()`, `today()` and `random()` are refused in every expression, because a report renders the same from the same data.
A diagnostic's position is left out past a read written longer than plainly, such as `row["amount"]`.
Every keystroke compiles every expression, and what that costs is not measured.
Division, a double literal, `double()` and `matches()` are refused in expressions; an author writes `divide(dec(a), dec(b), places)` and `dec("…")` instead.
A field the report does not declare is refused, so a host sends exactly what the report reads.
A decimal travels only as a string, and one sent as a JavaScript number is refused.
A render reads at most 100,000 detail rows, and a final render refuses data its provider calls incomplete.
An image's bytes are not checked against their digest: the host's lookup is trusted to return what the digest pins.
A declared rounding is applied once to each group's total and once to the report's, so rounded subtotals need not add up to the rounded total.
Grouping marks, currency symbols and month names are the JavaScript engine's ICU's, so the same report can print differently on two engines.
The expression budget was measured on one machine, and on another a render within it takes what that machine takes.
An expression cannot read an image field, not even to ask whether it is null.
A preview's label is English, whatever the report's locale.

One font, Roboto, for everything but a QR-bill's slip and an EPC QR code's caption: CJK, Hebrew, Arabic, Thai, emoji and fr-FR amounts are refused in printed text, as are the `serif` and `mono` families.
A word wider than its table column is refused, never broken: the template gives the column the width, or the text goes in a paragraph.
A render cannot be stopped while pdfmake lays out a pass; a host that must stop one at once runs it in a worker it can terminate, and none is built.
The renderer reads pdfmake internals that are not its API, at one exact pdfmake version, so a pdfmake upgrade reaches an installation only through a release of this module whose tests ran on it.
A kept block's first and last rows are named destinations in the PDF, two to a block.
A table inside a frame, or one whose rows may split across pages, is laid out once per page break rather than planned.
A body that fits its least height but not its real one is measured whole before it is refused.
A touch device gets no drag in the Angular builder, which binds HTML drag and drop, and the two builders' drag thresholds differ.
The session's step labels are English sentences, whatever language its editors speak.

Where the shared scenarios and the Studio's comparison of the two builders' accessible trees stop -- each framework's pointer gesture, a state neither takes the builders to -- the builders are held to each other by their own tests and by the core's README, which nothing executes.

The two builders' accessible trees are compared in jsdom and in Chromium alone, at the states the Studio's parity test and its browser gate take them to, so a difference only Firefox or WebKit computes, or one at a state neither reaches, is found by nobody.

The builders' own suites run in jsdom: layout, contrast, target size and a real pointer's drag are measured only through the Studio, in Chromium, and the pictures in the builders' own READMEs are taken by hand.
No PDF viewer is published: the Studio's PDF.js viewer stays inside the private app, so a host shows a report's PDF with a viewer of its own.

A host that wants formancy.ai's admin look for the builder copies the Studio's builder.css rules, and imports `@formancy/themes/room.css` for the colours as the Studio does (0034); the room alone gives the workbench's own shapes in the room's colours.
The browser gate measures the Studio in Chromium alone, so layout, contrast, target size and a pointer's drag are not measured in Firefox or WebKit.
A README picture of the Studio is held to the text its parts show, not to its pixels, so a change of colour or layout alone, or a quoted line scrolled out of its part, is seen only by looking.
A release names what its own run tested: a dependency version, a framework release or a Node that no job of that run used was not tested, and nothing in the product refuses it.

The publish job has run twice, for 0.1.0 and 0.2.0, where every step succeeded; run again over versions npm already holds, which is how a release recovers from a failed GitHub release, it has never run, and the workflows test holds its shape and not its behaviour.

The getting-started guide's pages are compiled, drawn on a server and bundled for a browser by the install gate, never mounted in one: the React page's preview effect, the PDF in its iframe, a press of Save and the Angular entry's bootstrap are not run.
The guide's angular.json lines and the server routes its pages call are checked by nothing, and its Angular page has no preview.

Data read through the Formancy Data provider is best-effort: the header, each page of lines and each label are read at different moments, so a line changed between two pages can be printed twice or not at all, and every render's manifest says best-effort.
Running the Formancy Data provider in production needs a Formancy Data production licence as well as Report's, because it depends on Data's source-available packages.
A float column, a repeater's rows and an image field cannot be printed from Formancy Data, and a lookup whose label the person may not see refuses the whole report rather than print nothing.

A report of many lines takes one list request for every 50 of them and one label request for every 50 distinct values of each lookup, each asking Data's policy again; how long that takes has not been measured.
The Formancy Data provider has run against a server that answers Data 0.1.0's routes in Data's shapes, never against a real Data server, its policy or its databases.

The SBOM names the published packages and what npm installed with them during the release's run, without the peers a host brings; past the runtime dependencies and upstream packages the release report names, each version in it is what npm resolved then, which no suite ran.

The Studio at formancy.ai/report/ is main's, built and deployed by Cloudflare on every push to main without waiting for that commit's CI, so it can show what no release holds yet; nothing in this repository checks that a build deployed or what the address serves.
A pane hidden in a builder, and the Studio's Preview, stay hidden only while the editor lives: nothing remembers them, and a reload or a new editor shows every pane.
A pane is hidden whole or shown at the workbench's width, never resized.
A report that holds a QR code is refused whole by 0.1.0, which does not know the kind, so a report saved with one opens only in a release that has it.
A QR code takes no colour or fill of its own, holds no page number or count, and cannot stand in a table's cells, so a coloured code or a code per row cannot be written.
A QR code is drawn black on white, square and without a logo, its error correction level the only choice, and its version, mask and mode the encoder's.

A QR code component is neither a Swiss QR-bill nor an EPC QR code: it draws no Swiss cross and no frame, and nothing checks the syntax of what it holds; a bill is a report's payment part (0022), and a SEPA credit transfer's code an `epcQrCode` (0025).

In a preview, a QR code whose content lacks a value, or holds one that is null, encodes what is left and is not marked as a preview's, so it can scan to a shorter reference than the final render, which refuses it.

A QR code component's modules are never drawn finer than 0.4 mm, the minimum of SIX's QR-bill guidelines (version 2.3, section 6.3) taken as a general one and measured on no printer or phone, so a small square with long text is refused where some printers might have printed it, and so is a component the size of the largest code those guidelines print, at 0.393 mm a module, which a QR-bill's own code is drawn at (0022).
A QR code marks no character set: ZXing reads its text as UTF-8, but a reader that keeps to ISO/IEC 18004's default of ISO/IEC 8859-1 reads an umlaut or the euro sign as other characters.
What a QR code encodes is not in the PDF's text, so search, copy and a screen reader find nothing there unless the template prints it beside the code.

The renderer depends on uqr 0.1.3 at an exact version, and on that version's behaviour, such as the error it throws for text too long, so a fix to the QR encoder reaches an installation only through a release of this module whose tests ran on it.
That a QR code scans is shown by ZXing reading the page as PDF.js draws it, never by a phone's camera or a printed page.

The pages at formancy.ai/report/<lang>/ are main's, deployed with the Studio, and name the changelog's newest release from the moment its release commit reaches main, before the tag has published the packages.
Nothing in this repository submits the pages' sitemap to a search engine or checks that formancy.ai's robots.txt lets them be crawled: the rightsholder submits it in Google Search Console by hand.

The pages' reflow down to 320 pixels and their colour contrast were measured in Chromium by hand, not by a gate, so a change to the pages or to the Studio's stylesheets they import is not measured in a browser in CI.
What a page says of the product, beyond the facts it reads from the repository's files, and whether a translation says what the English says, are held by review, not by a test.
A report with a payment part is refused whole by 0.1.0, as `unknown-property`, so a report saved with a QR-bill opens only in a release that has one.

A report carries at most one QR-bill, printed at the foot of its last page and only on an A4 page in portrait, with its top margin above the slip's top, so a report of several invoices cannot carry one for each.

A QR-bill has no ultimate creditor, no alternative procedures and no bill "not for payment", and a EUR bill to a QR-IBAN with a QR reference, which version 2.3 of SIX's guidelines allows until November 2027, is refused under version 2.4's rule.

A QR-bill's country is checked as two capital letters, not against the codes ISO 3166-1 assigns, its billing information only for the // and the two characters naming its syntax it begins with, its postal codes not for a country's prefix, which SIX forbids, and nothing checks that the account is the creditor's.
Neither builder edits a QR-bill: the design view shows where its slip prints, the bill is written in the report's definition, and its diagnostics are listed as the report's, with no row to select.

The editor refuses a top margin that reaches into a QR-bill's slip and nothing more: a page header, or the 10.24 pt line of the instruction to separate, reaching into it is refused only when the report renders, by the same rule, since only a render measures them.
A QR-bill's amount is never rounded: one with more than two decimals is refused, so the template rounds the total it asks for.
A preview is refused when the values it lacks leave its QR-bill breaking one of SIX's rules, where any other missing value prints as nothing and is warned of.
A null in a QR-bill's debtor refuses a final render, so whether a bill names its payer is the template's choice and never a row's.
A QR-bill's amount that may be null is typed by the editor as a value of either kind, so a nullable integer field passes its diagnostics and is refused only when the report renders.
A QR-bill's text is printed at SIX's recommended sizes and never shrunk, so an address or a message taller than its section is refused rather than printed smaller.

A QR-bill whose texts SIX's rules accept is still refused by the renderer when its code's UTF-8 is longer than the 997 bytes SIX's largest code holds, a long bill of accented letters or euro signs, since the editor and the runtime count characters and not bytes.
A QR-bill's billing information is printed beside its message whenever it has one, since nothing can tell whether it holds personal data.

Where SIX gives no figure the slip is this module's choice: the Swiss cross as schoero's generator draws SIX's logo, the scissors symbol's drawing, its size and place after manuelbl's generator, the lines' weight, the instruction's size and place, and a foreign country's printed form.
The renderer's package carries Liberation Sans twice, as TrueType for Node and as base64 for the browser, which took it from 268,045 bytes unpacked at 0.1.0 to 2,307,611 on 17 October 2026.

A browser host gets Liberation Sans as a chunk of 1.1 MB, 519 kB gzipped, loaded with its first QR-bill or captioned EPC QR code (0025), or in every page if its bundler does not split dynamic imports; a host that bundles the Node entry copies the font files beside it. A chunk that failed to load is asked for again by the next bill or captioned code, but whether the browser fetches it again is the browser's, and a chunk a deploy removed fails every bill and captioned code until the page reloads.
A QR-bill makes a render slower and larger: the invoice starter took 263 to 300 ms and 53,730 bytes, against 70 to 82 ms and 23,985 bytes without its bill, on one machine on 17 October 2026.
That a QR-bill is paid is not tested: its code is read by ZXing from the page PDF.js draws, never by a bank's scanner or a banking app, and no slip has been printed.

The Studio and the product pages at formancy.ai/report/ each serve their own copy of their faces, 887,348 bytes in 59 files per build on 2026-10-17, fallbacks for browsers without WOFF2 among them, so a reader who goes from a page to the Studio fetches the faces again.

A reader with a font named Archivo installed sees the Studio's and the pages' headings in it, perhaps without its width axis, because the room's stack names Archivo before the Archivo Variable the build serves.
That a product page asks no other site for anything rests on the suite reading its HTML and stylesheet, not on a browser watching its requests, which only the Studio has.

The QR-bill page, formancy.ai/report/de/qr-rechnung/ and its translations, says whether the newest release holds the bill, 0.2.0 being the first that does, and the pages refuse to render once CHANGELOG.md names a release after the one its status was written against, so every release commit fails the pages' suite until that page's status is written again.

From the merge of a release commit until its tag publishes the packages, the QR-bill page says the getting-started guide installs that release, which npm does not serve yet: a reader who follows it installs the release before, and for 0.2.0 that is 0.1.0, which refuses a report with a QR-bill.

Of the invoice's samples, only the German one is a starter the Studio offers: the French, Italian and English samples are shown on the QR-bill page as pictures, and live in report-corpus, which is never published.

A QR-bill in French prints its instruction to separate as "A détacher avant le versement", as the English edition of version 2.4 of SIX's guidelines tables it, where the French edition of version 2.3 writes "À détacher".

A QR-bill's PDF is the bill SIX's guidelines describe for paying by e-banking or mobile banking, its lines marked with the scissors or the instruction to separate; a bill sent on paper must be printed on white, perforated paper (sections 3.1, 3.3 and 3.7 of the guidelines' version 2.4), which nothing in this module sees.

The invoice samples print their amounts, quantities and dates as the ICU data of the Node that renders them formats fr-CH, it-CH and en-CH, so a Node whose ICU formats them otherwise fails the samples' pictures, and then the QR-bill page's quotes, until the pictures are taken again.
A report that holds an EPC QR code is refused whole by 0.1.0, which does not know the kind, so a report saved with one opens only in a release that has it.

An EPC QR code pays a SEPA credit transfer in euro and nothing else: no instant transfer, no other currency, no character set but UTF-8, and no structured reference but an ISO 11649 creditor reference, so a Belgian structured communication goes in its text.
An EPC QR code's amount is a decimal with no currency, and nothing checks that the value a template binds to it is in euro, so a total the report prints in francs is asked for as so many euros.

An EPC QR code's purpose is four capital letters, not checked against ISO 20022's purpose codes, and its BIC may hold digits among its first four characters on the EPC's alphanumeric data type alone, which nothing here checked against ISO 9362.

Which countries an EPC QR code pays to, and each one's IBAN length, is a table recorded on 17 October 2026 from EPC409-09 version 8.0 and, for the lengths, python-stdnum's copy of release 101 of SWIFT's IBAN Registry, whose own file was not read, so a country joining SEPA or a length the registry changes reaches an installation only through a release of this module.

An account's place is read from its IBAN's country, so an EPC QR code paying a French IBAN of a bank in Saint Pierre and Miquelon, which is outside the EEA, is taken without the BIC the EPC asks for there, and one of a bank in New Caledonia, French Polynesia or Wallis and Futuna, which EPC409-09 does not list, as a transfer within SEPA.

An EPC QR code needs a BIC only for an account outside the EEA, though the EPC keeps it mandatory wherever a bank outside the EEA takes part, the payer's among them, so a code without one may be refused by a payer's bank in Switzerland or Britain.

An EPC QR code's BIC is refused when it is of another country than its IBAN, an inference from EPC409-09's territory codes that neither EPC document states, so an account whose bank's BIC is another country's is refused.
An EPC QR code refuses a QR-IBAN, by SIX's rule that one is paid by a QR-bill in francs with a QR reference, not by the EPC's.

Nothing in the format pins an EPC QR code to the lower edge of the last page, where Austria's PSA asks for it: a code in the page footer prints on every page, and one in the summary where the body ends.

Nothing checks that a template prints an EPC QR code's beneficiary, IBAN and amount beside it in plain text, as the EPC means the code to be printed, and the code carries no bank's or scheme's brand name or logo.
An EPC QR code's amount is never rounded: one with more than two decimals is refused, so the template rounds the total it asks for.

An optional text of an EPC QR code that the data gives empty, blank or null is left out of the code rather than refused, in a final render as in a preview, so a missing BIC is no BIC and a missing reference a code without one, where a QR-bill's optional texts refuse a null in a final render.
A preview is refused when the values it lacks leave an EPC QR code without a text the EPC requires, where any other missing value prints as nothing and is warned of.
An EPC QR code is held to the EPC's 331 bytes once its data is known, so a code whose data makes it too long is refused by the render, not by the editor.

Austria's frame and "Zahlen mit Code" are an option: a code without them is held to the 0.4 mm floor of every QR code and to no largest module, where the PSA asks 15 to 20 mil of every code it prints, and a code with them may have modules as fine as 0.381 mm.

A captioned EPC QR code is printed only in a square of 68.06 to 118.6 pt (24.0 to 41.8 mm), and at a version raised until its modules are at most 20 mil, so its symbol can be larger than its payload needs.

The frame around a captioned EPC QR code reaches half a module into ISO/IEC 18004's quiet zone at its corners, as the PSA's own figure does, and the frame's line, its place and the caption's size are this module's choices within the bounds the PSA gives.

An EPC QR code makes a render slower and larger: the euro invoice starter took 86 to 116 ms and 31,487 bytes with its code, 114 to 135 ms and 38,207 bytes with Austria's caption, and 74 to 81 ms and 26,348 bytes without the code, on one machine on 17 October 2026.

In the builders an EPC QR code's text of several runs, or a bound one, cannot be removed and no run can be added, a square too small for the frame is refused in points in a field edited in millimetres, and the German and French names of its fields, and what its empty BIC field says, are no native speaker's.

In the builders' design view a component at the top of a narrow column at a container's right end, an EPC QR code beside its details among them, has its label printed over the container's, so that neither can be read.

That an EPC QR code is paid is not tested: its code is read by ZXing from the page PDF.js draws, never by a banking app, no code has been printed, and the EPC's guidelines are informative, so a bank need not read one at all.

0026.none: It decides how the repository documents its architecture and what holds those documents in pnpm test:repo; its costs fall on a contributor's pull request, and nothing in a published package, a release or the Studio changes with it.

limitations.says: A report with an e-invoice is refused whole by 0.1.0, as `unknown-property`, so a report saved with one opens only in a release that has it.

An e-invoice is EN 16931's profile of Factur-X 1.09.2 / ZUGFeRD 2.5.2 alone, a commercial invoice (380) in euro with the VAT categories S, E and AE and no allowances or charges, so a credit note, another currency, a 0 % supply EN 16931 codes Z, an intra-EU supply, XRechnung and a structured Skonto cannot be invoiced, and a discount is written as a line of negative quantity at a positive price.

An e-invoice's units, countries, VAT prefixes and schemes come from closed lists that someone chose, narrower than CEN's and held to CEN's 1.3.17 and the pinned 1.3.16 lists on 17 October 2026, so a code CEN takes and the lists do not, a packaging unit, Northern Ireland's XI or a seller's country outside Europe, is refused.

An e-invoice's lines are printed by four columns of the table over the detail dataset, its name, quantity, net price and net amount, none of which, nor the table, may be hidden, so an invoice that shows no unit price cannot be an e-invoice.
The title of a report with an e-invoice cannot hold `&`, `<` or `>`, which its page can print.

An e-invoice's payment account and its BIC are held to the EPC QR code's IBAN and BIC rules for a credit transfer (30) as for a SEPA credit transfer (58), so a credit transfer to an account or a bank outside SEPA is refused.
A standard rated VAT category's rate is 0.5 or more, since BR-CO-17 rounds a rate below it to 0 and then wants a tax that rounds to 0.
The seller's and the buyer's street, post code and city are needed, as § 14 Abs. 4 Satz 1 Nr. 1 UStG asks, where EN 16931 needs only the country, so an address without a post code cannot be written.

An invoice number, a registration identifier, a post code, a BIC or a line's identifier holding a tab, a line break, two spaces in a row or a space at either end is refused, never trimmed, since the XML writes each as a token a schema-aware reader collapses, so data padded with blanks is refused.

Nothing checks that a payment code's BIC is an e-invoice's, an e-invoice's VAT identifiers past their country prefix, that a rate is the right one for a line, or that an exemption reason says what the law says, so an invoice wrong in what it states can pass every rule.

An e-invoice is made for Germany: France's XP Z12-012 was not read, the buyer's SIREN is the only one of its four mandatory details the XML holds, and no French platform's acceptance of the file is known.

What a Factur-X PDF says of its XML, the relationship `Alternative`, the conformance level and the XMP's namespace, prefix and values, rests on a transcription of the Factur-X 1.09.2 specification and not on the specification, whose registration nobody here has made, and the release's XSD and schematron are Mustang 2.26.0's copies of FeRD's, which sit behind the same registration.

In a report with an e-invoice the editing core refuses a page that prints none of a total the XML holds, or that prints a total or a line's net amount at fewer than two places or in another currency, a net price in another currency, or an item's name in another case, but sees only that a run reads a total and its format, not what else the run prints with it or whether its condition holds.
An e-invoice's totals cannot be read in an aggregate, in the e-invoice's own texts or in the columns that print its lines, so its remittance information cannot quote the amount due.
The editing core types an e-invoice's dates as text, so an expression that gives a string that is no date passes its diagnostics and is refused only when the report renders.
Neither builder edits an e-invoice, which is written in the report's definition, and the Studio offers none of the corpus's e-invoice samples.
An e-invoice's VAT is rounded once per category, half away from zero, so an ERP that rounds each line's VAT may differ from it by up to half a cent a line.
An e-invoice's line net amounts and its paid amount are whole cents and never rounded, so a template rounds where it computes a line.

An e-invoice's line net amount is refused unless it is its quantity times its net price rounded once to the cent, in a preview too, so a price per hundred, a line discount or an amount rounded otherwise cannot be written.

An e-invoice's line identifier is refused where an earlier line has it, and a quantity or a net price where its column prints fewer places than the data gives, so an article number shared by two lines cannot be a line's identifier and a column cannot round what the XML holds.

Neither a due date nor payment terms is asked of an e-invoice with an amount due, which CEN's 1.3.15 refused as BR-CO-25 and its 1.3.16 does not, so a receiver that validates against 1.3.15 refuses such a file.
A QR-bill printed with an e-invoice asks for euro, so one paid to a QR-IBAN with a QR reference, which SIX keeps for francs, cannot be printed with one.

Every host that bundles report-spec, report-core and report-runtime carries the e-invoice's rules and writer, whether its reports have one or not: measured on 17 October 2026 with esbuild 0.28.2 from each package's source, they grew from 145,932 to 194,092 bytes minified and from 49,511 to 65,008 gzipped.
A preview of an e-invoice writes no XML, warns that it writes none and labels every page, so only a final render writes the invoice.
A QR-bill or an EPC QR code printed with an e-invoice is refused unless it asks for the amount due, or leaves the amount to the payer, and asks to be paid to the e-invoice's account.
An e-invoice with an invoicing period and no delivery date writes the delivery element the XSD requires empty, which Mustang's schematron warns of as PEPPOL-EN16931-R008.

An e-invoice's XML has no bound but the 100,000 detail rows a render reads at most: at that many lines it held 117,280,919 bytes, and resolving took a median of 5.4 s against 2.0 s without it, over five runs from the built package on Node 24.21.0 and an Intel i9-10900K on 17 October 2026.

A renderer that predates e-invoices, 0.1.0's among them, would draw a resolved e-invoice as a plain PDF, which only two runtimes in one install could hand it, since the packages pin each other exactly.

The e-invoice gate's Mustang 2.26.0 and KoSIT 1.6.3 run CEN's 1.3.16 artefacts, where report-spec's rules follow 1.3.17, and on 17 October 2026 the gate had run on Windows alone, on Zulu 25 and Temurin 17, never in CI, where the release report holds it to the register's Java major version and a machine's run is held to none.

The e-invoice's closed lists hold codes copied out of CEN/TC 434's EUPL-1.2 artefacts, and the gate's recorded KoSIT and Mustang reports quote CEN's rule texts, and whether either is acceptable under 0006 is the rightsholder's open question.

The e-invoice gate's downloads carry works under their own licences, Saxon, veraPDF under the GPL or the MPL, and CEN's EUPL-1.2 schematron, which run in CI, were not reviewed one by one, and no package carries.
The ZUGFeRD and Factur-X marks are AWV e.V.'s, and whether naming them, as the e-invoice samples' title and the code do, meets their owner's conditions has not been read.

From the merge of a release commit until its tag publishes the packages, the EPC QR code page says the getting-started guide installs that release, which npm does not serve yet: a reader who follows it installs the release before, and for 0.2.0 that is 0.1.0, which refuses a report with an EPC QR code.

Of the euro invoice's samples, only the German one is a starter the Studio offers: the Austrian, French, Italian, Spanish, Dutch and Irish samples are shown on the EPC QR code page as pictures, and live in report-corpus, which is never published.

The euro invoice's samples are no tax advice: each prints its country's standard VAT rate as the EU's Your Europe table gave it on 17 October 2026, nothing reads the rates again, that a sale of parts takes that rate is this module's reading and no tax adviser's, and they may lack what their countries' invoicing law asks: none states a legal guarantee of conformity, the Spanish holds at most as a simplified invoice, without its customer's NIF, the Italian gives no codice fiscale, and the Italian, Dutch and Austrian no company register's number.

The euro invoice's samples are PDFs and no e-invoice: none is an XRechnung, ZUGFeRD, Factur-X or FatturaPA, the Italian sample says it is a courtesy copy of an electronic invoice, and the Spanish one prints no Verifactu code.

The EPC QR code page names the Studio's starter "Euro invoice", its picker's "Starter" and its palette's "EPC payment code" as words nothing here reads, and its hero opens the Studio at its first starter, not at the euro invoice.

The euro invoice's samples print their amounts and dates as the ICU data of the Node that renders them formats de-AT, fr-FR, it-IT, es-ES, nl-NL and en-IE, so a Node whose ICU formats them otherwise fails the samples' pictures, and then the EPC QR code page's quotes, until the pictures are taken again.

The euro invoice samples' words in German for Austria, French, Italian, Spanish, Dutch and English, and the EPC QR code page's in German, French, Italian and English, are no native speaker's, and nobody here reads the Spanish or the Dutch.

The Italian and Irish samples' accounts are known only to have the right check digits: the Banca d'Italia's register and a list of Irish sort codes could not be read on 17 October 2026, so nothing shows that no bank keeps their bank codes, as the Austrian, French, Spanish and Dutch registers showed for theirs.

The euro invoice samples' firms, customers and addresses are invented, and nobody checked that no business is at those addresses; that each VAT number fails its country's check was computed once, on 17 October 2026, and no test holds it.

The EPC QR code page's reflow down to 320 pixels and its colour contrast were measured in Chromium by hand on 17 October 2026, with every other page's, and by no gate, so a later change to a page is measured in a browser by nobody.

The Studio's Preview starts over, printed again at its first page, fitted to the width and in preview mode, each time it takes the design view's place, the framework is switched below 2053 pixels or the window crosses 2052, and the design view it swaps with loses its scroll position.

The Studio's Preview in the builder's middle keeps the header it has beside the builder: its heading, status and tools take 185 pixels of the middle at 1366 by 768 and 1440 by 900, its tools in two rows, and 141 at 1920 by 1080, measured on 18 October 2026.

When the Preview takes the design view's place, the builder's live region, saying how to bring the design view back, and the Preview's own status speak at the same time.

The README's pictures show the Studio past 2052 pixels and at 390, never with the Preview in the builder's middle at a laptop's width, since the camera takes no width between the Studio's breakpoints.

A report that declares an SVG asset is refused whole by 0.1.0, as `not-one-of` on its media type, and an image field's SVG by 0.1.0's runtime, so a report saved with one opens only in a release that has it.

An SVG asset holds drawing elements alone: text, embedded pictures, `use`, `symbol`, patterns, masks, markers, filters, `foreignObject`, `switch` and conditional-processing attributes are refused, so a logo with live lettering, an icon sprite or an Illustrator file saved with its editing capabilities is refused until it is exported again, its text converted to outlines.

Of thirteen invented samples of what drawing programs write, five are refused -- live text from Illustrator and Sketch, Illustrator's editing capabilities and its CS-era entities, and Canva's lettering, which Canva writes as `symbol` and `use` and cannot outline itself -- and a Canva logo of five shapes or more is refused too, since Canva clips every shape and a drawing may make four units of transparency groups; the samples were never compared with a real export.

A colour with an alpha, `hsl()`, `transparent` and the system colours are refused in an SVG rather than turned into an opacity; `#rgb`, `#rrggbb`, `rgb()` and CSS Color 4's names are read, each written as `#rrggbb`.
A hidden layer of an SVG that holds text or a filter is refused though it draws nothing, since an element is judged before CSS says it is hidden.

An SVG of more than 10,000 weighted segments -- a line 1, a curve 3, a stroke twice more -- is refused, so a detailed crest or a long outlined lettering may need simplifying in its drawing program before it is approved: the bound was lowered from 30,000 when a path every segment of which crosses its box was found to cost a reader 1.15 to 1.84 s at 30,000, against 0.12 to 0.55 s at 10,000, measured on 18 October 2026.

Stylesheets in an SVG are bounded by the work of their cascade as well as by their selectors, so a drawing whose elements each hold a combination of classes of their own under many rules is refused, though no export sampled comes near it.

An SVG asset may be a mebibyte as it comes and as `cleanSvg` writes it, and the written form can be several times the file, so a drawing whose cleaned form would pass a mebibyte is refused when it is approved.

An approved SVG is the drawing `cleanSvg` writes, not the file as it came: comments, metadata, editor layers, scripts, links' addresses and what never draws are removed when it is approved, and an SVG in any other form is refused when it prints, so a host shows its approver the cleaned drawing or the PDF, never the file as uploaded, which a browser draws otherwise.

An SVG in a page header or footer is drawn again on every page, so a detailed logo grows the PDF and the render with every page: a header logo of 30,000 lines took a 32-page render 2.8 s longer than one of a single rectangle, and each translucent gradient wrote about 1.8 kB more a page, on one machine on 18 October 2026; every 32 bytes of a drawing count too, since pdfmake and its converter read the whole text again each time it is drawn.

A render may draw `MAX_SVG_DRAWING` units of SVG, an image in a page region counted on every page `maxPages` allows and not on the pages printed, so at a limit of 200 pages a header logo may cost 5,000 units however short the report: a logo of 9,999 short lines, the most one drawing may hold, costs 12,152 and may head a report of 82 pages at most, which the Studio's Preview, limited to 40, draws and a render limited to 200 refuses.

Every SVG image of a body is held to the bounds of one drawing as though all fell on one page, so a logo of three units of transparency groups printed twice in a body is refused, wherever the two land.

pdfmake's SVG converter draws every clip path and translucent gradient as a transparency group the size of the page, and a rasteriser pays for a segment on every row of pixels it spans, so the worst drawing the bounds accept, 15 mm square, added 0.19 s to a page drawn at a device pixel ratio of 1 and 0.39 s at 2, and page-wide 0.27 s and 0.55 s, in headless Chromium on 18 October 2026, against 0.06 to 0.09 s for a starter page, in every reader of the PDF and in the Studio's Preview on every edit.

In an e-invoice, whose PDF/A-3 holds an integer to 2,147,483,647 and nests the graphics state 28 deep, an SVG is refused as `unsupported`, naming the image, where the numbers the converter would write for it could pass that less a margin of 5.7 % for rounding, or where it nests deeper: a logo whose clips or transparency are drawn under a shrink of 10^6 is refused on A4 below 41.6 pt square, one whose gradient inside a group grows as far as the group shrinks at any size, one whose arc has radii far too short for its ends, or whose path chains thousands of reflected quadratics, at any size, and one nested more than 28 graphics states deep in one content stream at any size; each draws in a report that is no e-invoice, so a template finds out at an e-invoice's render.

Of the invented exporter samples the cleaner accepts, each makes its page-sized groups under no matrix that shrinks them and nests five graphics states deep at most, so an e-invoice refuses none of them for its nesting, nor for its groups but as the image's own box shrinks; no real exporter's file has been measured.

In every report, a gradient is refused at approval as `out-of-range` where its matrix, in any box inside its shape's, could pass 10^6, since svg-to-pdfkit draws it in the box of the outline and the cleaner holds a curve by its control points: a drawing whose gradient cancels against its shape's box only in the box of the control points is refused, where only that box was held before.
That an SVG prints as a browser draws it is held by report-spec's tables and by review; no browser's drawing of an asset is compared with the PDF.

An e-invoice's SVG is held to PDF/A by a bound on the numbers the converter will write, never by reading its PDF back at print, and the bound assumes the converter's arithmetic strays from the cleaner's by no more than its margin, which matrices built to cancel one another term by term could defeat, and which nothing holds; the tests and the e-invoice gate read the numbers back, veraPDF none in a soft mask's group, a clip's.

What an SVG costs to clean, to draw and to paint was measured on one shared machine on 18 October 2026, under Node and in a headless Chromium drawing in software, and not in Firefox, WebKit, a browser drawing on a GPU or CI, so another reader may pay more for the worst drawing the bounds accept; the one time a gate holds, the worst drawing's raster, is held as a ratio to a starter page's in the same process, so that a slower runner is not a slower drawing.

An e-invoice is drawn as a PDF/A-3b, the one level pdfmake and PDFKit reach, so its PDF has no structure tree and is no tagged, accessible PDF, and a receiver who asks for PDF/A-3a or 3u gets level b.

A CMYK JPEG, an asset's or a field's, is refused in a final render of an e-invoice, naming the image, since its PDF/A-3b's output intent is sRGB, while its preview, which is no PDF/A, draws it, so an author finds out only at the final render.

A JPEG that PDFKit would read otherwise than its frame header says -- a JPG or DAC segment before the frame header, as arithmetic coding may write its DAC segment, a second frame header, or a frame of other than 1, 3 or 4 components -- is refused as `invalid-asset` in every report, where 0.1.0 drew it wrong, so a template that holds one stops rendering.

A PNG whose transparency is a colour key is drawn in every report as PDFKit's PNG reader, png-js 1.1.0, reads it: a grey key by its high byte, so another grey may be drawn transparent, and an RGB key as twelve numbers where a PDF reader wants six, which a reader may ignore.

The renderer refuses an e-invoice whose XML holds a lone surrogate, or whose title holds `&`, `<`, `>` or a character XML 1.0 cannot write, naming `info.title`, so a document a host builds otherwise than the runtime resolves one is refused where PDFKit would write a PDF that is no PDF/A.

An e-invoice's PDF carries the embedded file's /CheckSum as PDFKit writes it, its MD5 in 32 hexadecimal digits where ISO 32000-1 asks for 16 bytes, and a trailer /ID shared with every PDF of its title and creation date, which PDFKit derives it from.

A render of an e-invoice reads PDFKit's ICC profile from `data/sRGB_IEC61966_2_1.icc` beside PDFKit's own code, with `fs` and outside pdfmake's access policy, so a host that bundles the Node entry puts that file where the bundled PDFKit's `__dirname` points, or every e-invoice render fails, which nobody here has tried.

No validator in the e-invoice gate reads the namespace of an e-invoice's fx properties, which the transcription it rests on gives two ways, with `:invoice` in its section 6.3.1 and without it in BR-HYBRID-04, so if the specification means the one the renderer does not write, every e-invoice carries the wrong one unseen.

No validator compares an e-invoice's XMP conformance level with its XML's profile: the gate's own reading holds it for the PDFs the gate draws, and a receiver who runs Mustang or veraPDF alone would not see a level its XML does not have.

The browser entry's PDF/A-3b is drawn by pdfmake's browser build in Node in the tests and never in a browser, and its output intent is the profile that build carries as base64, which the dependency guard cannot read and a test holds to the reviewed one.

An e-invoice drawn as a PDF/A-3b is 8,497 to 8,564 bytes larger than the same report drawn plain: the corpus's samples were 36,712 to 37,801 bytes against 28,215 to 29,237, and their medians of nine renders 83 to 91 ms against 81 to 94 ms, within the noise of a machine running other work, measured on 18 October 2026 from the built packages on Node 24.21.0 and an Intel i9-10900K.

An e-invoice's page is held to the XML its PDF embeds for the corpus's three samples alone, and only those samples' XML, their PDFs and variants that carry the first sample's XML on the starters' pages and on a page of every image kind go through Mustang, KoSIT and veraPDF, so a customer's template is held by the rules and by the check that each total is printed.

The e-invoice gate needs a Java at least as new as each JAR's `java` in its register and 86,368,974 bytes of downloads, each pinned by its SHA-256, so a release of Mustang, KoSIT or veraPDF reaches the gate only through a change to its register.

Mustang 2.26.0 checks neither an embedded file's declared /CheckSum and /Size nor its /AFRelationship, as the gate's three controls of them show, and exits 0 on a PDF whose XML is valid whatever its PDF/A says, so the gate reads Mustang's PDF part and veraPDF's report and counts the files with pdf-lib, and a receiver who runs Mustang alone sees less.

Every variant of the e-invoice gate is recorded by the digest of its PDF, so a change to what a starter, the fonts fixture or an image kind draws fails the e-invoice job until somebody with a Java runs the gate with `--record`.

The e-invoice gate drew and judged its PDFs on Windows alone, on 18 October 2026, on Zulu 25 and Temurin 17 and under Node 22 and 24, and never in CI, where their digests and any ERROR line Mustang logs on Linux have not been seen.

The install gate is the one place a PDFKit that a host's install resolves within pdfmake's `^0.19.1` is seen embedding an e-invoice and its profile, and the release report names only the packed packages' direct dependencies, so it never says which PDFKit a host got.

veraPDF, which the e-invoice gate runs over the PDFs, is under GPL-3.0-or-later OR MPL-2.0, which the dependency policy refuses for a package: it is admitted for the gate's runs at 1.30.3 alone, and no package carries it.

An ICC profile is admitted by the SHA-256 of its bytes and the licence sentence a review read, never by anything the file says, so a PDFKit that ships another profile stops the dependency guard until somebody reads it, and a profile inside a script or an image is not seen.

The quotation, the QR-bill invoice and the euro invoice starters, their samples and the e-invoice samples name an approved asset, the firm's mark, so a host that prints one hands over the mark's bytes by its id and digest, or the render is refused `missing-asset`.
The marked starters declare an SVG asset, which 0.1.0 refuses as `not-one-of`, so the quotation and invoice starters as 0.2.0 has them open only in a release that reads SVG.

The getting-started guide's `printPreview` takes the host's lookup of approved assets as a parameter, and its page reads them from a route of the host's server beside the sample, so a page that copied the guide's `printPreview` before passes none, and refuses a report that draws an asset -- the quotation starter with its mark -- as `missing-asset` until it passes one.

The starters' mark is an invented drawing that names no firm, 15 mm square at the top left of the first page, taking 54.52 pt of it, so the quotation's first page holds 25 line items where it held 27; a firm's own logo is a new asset in a new template release, as any logo is.
A person adds an image in a builder only where the host gave the editor a store for the bytes; without one the builders offer no Add image…, and a report's images are the host's alone to declare.

Adding an image checks its size, what its bytes are, a PNG's or a JPEG's structure with every chunk's CRC, and its sides, and an SVG whole; a PNG whose image data does not inflate to the scanlines its header promises, or a JPEG whose scan is corrupt, is added and kept, and refused as `invalid-asset` only when it prints.

A CMYK JPEG is refused when it is added to a report with an e-invoice, whose PDF/A-3b cannot hold one; one added before the report gains an e-invoice is refused only at its final render, as `unsupported`.

An added image's digest is taken on the page's main thread by @noble/hashes: in Chromium 156 on an i9-10900K, on 19 October 2026, 18 ms for 1 MiB, 91 ms for 5 MiB and 360 ms for 20 MiB, about six times Web Crypto's, and the whole add of a PNG of just under 20 MiB in the Studio about half a second, while the page does nothing else.

Removing an image, or undoing its addition, leaves its bytes in the host's store, since a redo needs them and `keep` is never called again; a host lets go of what no report it keeps names and no open session can declare again by an undo or a redo.

The asset id an add hands the host's `keep` is the one it means to declare, and another editor of the same session may declare it meanwhile for other bytes, the add then refused with the bytes kept under it; and the runtime checks no bytes against their digest. A store keys what it keeps by digest, or by id and digest, never by id alone, or a lookup could print another image unseen.
The editor waits for the host's `keep` to settle and takes no other image meanwhile: a `keep` that never settles leaves Add image… unavailable for as long as the editor lives, and nothing cancels it.

A file whose bytes the report declares already is declared nothing more, and its bytes go to the host's `keep` again under the id they are declared by, so that a report whose host lacks them can be given them: one more keep of bytes a host may hold.

An added image's id is read from its file's name -- the extension dropped, letters folded to plain Latin, anything else a hyphen, numbered as it stands where the name is taken, a second IMG_4711.png being img-4711-2 -- and reaches the report, its hash, the outline and the diagnostics, so a file named after a person names that person in the report; the builders offer no other id, and no way to rename one.
An image is added one at a time per editor, and one whose id another editor of the same session declared while the host kept it is refused as `changed`, to be added again.

The Studio keeps every image a person adds in the tab's memory, up to the format's own limits of 64 images of 20 MiB a report in each starter, never lets one go, and sends nothing anywhere; nothing measured where a tab gives out first, and a reload forgets them with the sessions.

The builders' scenarios find the hidden file input Add image… opens by reading the DOM, the one element they find otherwise than by role and accessible name, and Space on Add image… is pressed for the Angular builder only by the Studio's browser gate, in Chromium.

`@formancy/report-spec` depends on `@noble/hashes` at exactly 2.4.0, which `@formancy/spec` 0.6.0 brings at `^2.4.0`, so a fix to it reaches an installation only through a release of this module, and an upgrade of either may install two copies.

A consumer of `@formancy/report-data-provider` installs two releases of `@formancy/spec`, 0.6.0 through `@formancy/report-spec` and 0.5.0 through `@formancy/data-client` and `@formancy/data-core` 0.1.0, which pin it exactly, until Formancy Data releases against 0.6.0; no object of one reaches the other in the provider.

The Studio's demo and the product pages at formancy.ai/report/ wear formancy's room as `@formancy/themes` 0.6.0 has it, so a colour formancy moves after 0.6.0 reaches them only with the bump of `@formancy/themes` that takes the release that moves it.

The colours admin.css's rules type that formancy's room does not carry -- the dark ink on the skip link and the chosen builder, the problem's pink, the shade under the starter picker and the Preview's pages, white's tints -- are copies in the Studio's and the pages' stylesheets, so one formancy's admin moves reaches neither until somebody copies it again.

A host page that wears formancy's room imports `@formancy/themes/room.css` after `workbench.css`, as the Studio does; imported before it, the workbench's light defaults win and the builder's panes stay light in the dark room.

The order a document's images are written in rests on three details of PDFKit 0.19.1 that are not its API, and the renderer pins PDFKit at 0.19.1 so that npm gives pdfmake that release (0036); a host whose package manager places it otherwise, or that holds a PDFKit of its own, resolves pdfmake's `^0.19.1`. A later 0.19.x that moved one would print the same pages in bytes that may differ from one render to the next; one that kept `finalize` but called it otherwise on one of a PNG's three decodes would leave a render with such an image ahead of another never ending, neither printing nor refused. Either is found by the install gate at its next run rather than by the renderer's own suite, which runs on 0.19.1.

report-render-pdf declares PDFKit at exactly 0.19.1 and imports nothing of it, so that an install gives pdfmake that release. The install gate, which installs with npm into hosts that hold no PDFKit of their own, holds that pdfmake loads it; under pnpm or Yarn, or beside a host's own PDFKit, which copy pdfmake loads was not measured, and a host can hold it with its own overrides. A PDFKit release that fixed the image order would reach a host only with a release of the renderer that moved the pin.
